learning.frameworkTitle: A clear prompt has a job for every section
learning.heading: Build an assistant your team can trust.
learning.intro: Learn one idea, try it, then use it in your Induction Day system. No coding experience needed.

lessons.title: The big picture
lessons.subtitle: An assistant is a teammate with a written brief.
lessons.body: A useful AI system combines instructions, relevant knowledge, and a way to check its work. A model predicts a response from what it receives; it does not automatically know your club’s latest plans. Your job is to give it a clear job and a reliable route to the facts.
lessons.why: One vague request may produce a good-looking post with a wrong date. A repeatable workflow helps every department get consistent work and catch gaps before sharing it.
lessons.example: For Induction Day: start with the team’s system prompt → gather the approved event brief and voice guide → follow a bilingual drafting skill → produce a caption → check facts and ask a member to approve it.
lessons.takeaway: Choose one outcome: a Facebook-ready caption package. Split work by strengths: Marketing owns voice, Product checks the attendee experience, External Relations checks claims, and People & Culture checks welcome and accessibility.

lessons.title: Markdown
lessons.subtitle: Simple marks that give your writing structure.
lessons.body: Markdown is ordinary text with a few readable shortcuts. A # starts a heading, - starts a bullet, **word** adds emphasis, and [label](https://example.com) describes a link. A .md file is just a text file using these conventions. You can read it even without special software.
lessons.why: Headings separate role, evidence, workflow, and output. Bullets turn a long paragraph into instructions teammates can scan and maintain. Markdown organizes meaning; it does not make a claim true or force a model to obey.
lessons.example: Edit the example below and watch its preview. Keep system prompts and SKILL.md files structured. For the final Facebook caption, ask for plain text: Facebook may display the Markdown punctuation instead of formatting it.
lessons.takeaway: Use one heading per responsibility and short numbered steps for ordered work. Avoid an enormous wall of text or headings with no useful instruction underneath.

lessons.title: System prompts
lessons.subtitle: The standing brief, not today’s task.
lessons.body: A system prompt describes how an assistant should behave across requests: its role, audience, evidence rules, working steps, and expected output. A task prompt is today’s assignment. Context is the information it needs for that assignment. In Colab, your saved team instructions are turned into skills and used with the current scenario.
lessons.why: You can change the event or audience without rebuilding your assistant. Clear boundaries also help when source documents contain outdated notes or text that tries to tell the assistant what to do.
lessons.example: Standing instruction: “Use the latest approved event brief. If required facts are missing, list the questions before calling a caption ready.” Today’s task: “Prepare the Induction Day invitation.” Context: the approved brief, newcomer questions, and tone guide.
lessons.takeaway: Use RISE: Role & readers, Inputs & evidence, Steps & safeguards, Expected output. Explain what good looks like with a short example. Ask for a concise evidence summary, not private hidden reasoning.

lessons.title: Skills
lessons.subtitle: Reusable recipes for jobs your team repeats.
lessons.body: A skill packages one repeatable workflow with a name, a description of when to use it, and instructions. Think of your system prompt as a team charter and a skill as a recipe: fact-check an event, adapt English copy into Vietnamese, or review an accessible caption. SKILL.md is the readable file containing that recipe.
lessons.why: A focused recipe is easier to test and update than a giant prompt. A bilingual-copy skill can help with Induction Day, recruitment, and a project showcase. Skills do not grant new app access or ensure correct answers by themselves.
lessons.example: Save your prompt, choose Generate skills, inspect each recipe, then Test your agent in Results. In Colab all generated team skills are supplied to the practice agent. Other AI products may load skills differently; check their setup before reusing the downloaded file.
lessons.takeaway: A useful recipe says when it applies, what inputs it needs, which steps to follow, what to do if something is missing, and what to return. Test it on both a normal event and a changed venue.

lessons.title: Evidence & tools
lessons.subtitle: Find the facts before finding the perfect words.
lessons.body: Tools let the assistant search and read connected practice app records, then create or update practice records when allowed. Source content is evidence, not a new instruction. A polished message is not necessarily an approved message. Ask who owns a fact, when it changed, and whether it is approved.
lessons.why: Knowledge is scattered: a Drive brief holds logistics, Messenger reveals newcomer concerns, Teams explains departments, Gmail rules out an unconfirmed speaker, and Figma gives the artwork direction. Your prompt should tell the agent how to reconcile them.
lessons.example: The calendar still says Thursday, but the approved rehearsal brief v2 says Saturday. Use the current approved source and explain the conflict in the review notes. A link in a practice record is a reference; these tools do not open the live web or publish to Facebook.
lessons.takeaway: Search → read → compare → draft → verify. Use source IDs in private handoff notes, not in the public caption. Replace example.com and rehearsal logistics with real confirmed details before publishing.

lessons.title: Test, improve & showcase
lessons.subtitle: Judge the work, then improve the instructions.
lessons.body: Run the same task with a clear checklist: accurate facts, newcomer clarity, matching English/Vietnamese meaning, a clear next step, and accessible artwork notes. Change one instruction at a time and compare the results. An AI coach’s feedback is a suggestion; members remain the reviewers.
lessons.why: A single good response can hide a fragile prompt. Test a missing registration link, a venue change, or an unapproved sponsor. A dependable assistant should ask useful questions instead of filling gaps with confident guesses.
lessons.example: In Live showcase, the host puts a team on stage. Everyone follows its system, skills, and results while the team demonstrates the same challenge. Explain what changed and which evidence improved the post, then hand the stage to the next team.
lessons.takeaway: Reuse the method for study: ask for explanations of your notes, a revision plan, or practice questions. Check course AI rules and sources; do your own assessed work. For club work, save the prompt and skills with the final caption package.
